table.title: Social Media Use and Disordered Eating: The Mediating Role of Self-Esteem in Predicting Bulking and Cutting Among Young Men
table.research_questions:
Social Media use will predict disordered eating and bulking and cutting behaviour.
Self-esteem will mediate or moderate this relationship.
table.study_type: Observational Study - Data is collected from study subjects that are not randomly assigned to a treatment. This includes surveys, “natural experiments,” and regression discontinuity designs.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview: The study will use a quantitative, within participants, cross-sectional design (single-time-point online survey via Qualtrics).
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures:
Participants will be recruited through Swansea University SONA participant pool, as well as social media platforms and local gyms. 

SONA credits will be available as a compensation for Swansea University psychology students. 

Data will be collected using an anonymous online survey hosted on Qulatrics. 

Participants must be: 
 -Men (cis or trans),
-Aged between 18 and 25 years,
-Currently residing in the UK,
-Regularly using social media (Instagram, TikTok, etc.),
-Engaging in gym-based physical activity or muscle-building routines (e.g., weightlifting, resistance training),
-Able to read and understand English,
-Willing and able to provide informed consent.
table.sample_size: The study aims to recruit at least 70 participants, possibly 100. This sample size is based on recommendations for conducting multiple regression and mediation analyses, which require sufficient statistical power to detect medium effect sizes. According to power analysis guidelines (e.g., using G*Power), a minimum of 67 participants is needed to detect a medium effect.
table.sample_size_rationale: The sample size is based on recommendations for conducting multiple regression and mediation analyses, which require sufficient statistical power to detect medium effect sizes. According to G*Power software, a minimum of 67 participants is needed to detect a medium effect.
table.measured_variables:
Bulking and cutting behaviours, 
Disordered eating, 
Self-esteem,
Social media use.
table.statistical_tests: Correlation. Multiple regression. Mediation analysis. Moderation analysis.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: Data will be excluded if > 3 SD from the mean.
table.missing_data_handling: Participants with missing data on any measure will be excluded from analyses using that measure.

table.text: The regression model for restraint was not significant, F(2, 73) = 1.28, p = .284, with an 200 adjusted R² of .007, indicating that social media and self-esteem explained less than 1% of the 201 variance.

text.text: Bulking and cutting (caloric surplus and restriction) are increasingly common among young men but remain under-researched within disordered eating frameworks.
This study examined social media use and self-esteem as predictors, as well as their association with disordered eating and bulking and cutting behaviours.

Seventy-six physically active UK men aged 18-25 years (M = 22.07, SD = 2.07) completed online measures of social media use, self-esteem, disordered eating (restraint, eating concern, shape concern, weight concern), and bulking and cutting behaviours.
Higher social media use predicted higher eating concern (p = .003), while lower self-esteem predicted higher eating and shape concerns (p = .029, p = <.001).

text.text: Neither social media use nor self-esteem predicted restraint, bulking, or cutting.

text.text: Social media use and self-esteem appear to relate to specific disordered eating symptoms, whereas bulking and cutting may be more closely linked to restraint processes.
These findings support expanding conceptualisations of disordered eating in young men to include muscleoriented dietary behaviours and their distinct psychological pathways.

text.text: We hope that a better understanding of these unique processes in young men may inform the development of more targeted and effective interventions.
The study employed a cross-sectional correlational design.
We examined social media use as the predictor, self-esteem as a mediator, and five outcome variables (eating concern, shape concern, restraint, bulking, and cutting).
Participants (N = 76) were predominantly cisgender men (94.7%) and mostly White (63.2%), with the rest identifying as Asian, Black, Mixed, and Other.
About 78% identified as heterosexual.
An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power 3.1 [37].
text.formatted: An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power 3.1 <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37]</ref>.

text.text: A sample of 68 participants was required to detect medium effect size (f² = .15) with power = .80 at α = .05 in a multiple regression model with two predictors.
Therefore, the gathered sample provided sufficient power to test the hypothesis.
Recruitment took place between July 25 th and August 21 st 2025 via social media and community advertising.
Eligible participants were men aged 18-25 years, residing in the UK, active on social media, physically active, and proficient in English.
Participation was voluntary and where applicable participants were granted 1 SONA credit (online research participation system).
All participants completed a survey via Qualtrics (https://www.qualtrics.com/).

text.text: Social media use was assessed with the Self-report Habit Index (SRHI) [38], a 10-item measure, rated on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from1 = "Strongly Disagree" to7 = "Strongly Agree."

text.text: Participants responded to statements such as: "Browsing Social Media is something…" for example … "I do without thinking" or "That I would find hard not to do."
Higher mean scores indicated more frequent use.
In the present sample, SRHI showed excellent internal consistency (Cronbach's α = .91).
We used an adapted version of Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q) [39], a 21-item, 6-point Likert scale to assess eating disorder symptoms over the past 28 days.

text.text: The scale measured: Restraint, Eating Concern, and Shape Concern, with questions such as: "Have you tried to follow definite rules regarding your eating (for example, a calorie limit) in order to influence your shape or weight (whether or not you have succeeded)?"
Scores were calculated as mean, with higher scores reflecting greater eating pathology.
The measure showed good internal consistency (α = .80 for restraint, α = .81 for eating concern, α = .81 for shape concern), and the global score demonstrated good to excellent reliability (α = .86).

The Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (RSE) [41], a 10-item, 4-point Likert scale ranging from3 = "Strongly Agree" to0 = "Strongly Disagree" and items 2, 5, 6, 8, 9 reverse-scored is a well-validated measure of global self-esteem (Cronbach's α = .84).

text.text: Items included statements such as "I feel that I have a number of good qualities" and "At times I think I am no good at all."
We developed a bespoke 10-item self-report measure to assess engagement in bulking and cutting (see S1 Appendix).
It comprises two subscales (5 items each).
An example of bulking statement is: "I intentionally eat more calories than I burn to gain muscle mass."
In the cutting subscale an example statement is: "I track my calories to ensure I'm eating at a deficit."
Items are rated from0 = "Strongly disagree" to3 = "Strongly agree."
The score is calculated as a mean, with higher scores indicating greater engagement.
The Bulking and Cutting Behaviour Scale was informed by theoretical definitions of bulking and cutting [40, 42], and psychological research on body image and eating behaviours [43, 44].

Combined, the overall scale demonstrated good reliability (Cronbach's α = .72).

The study took 10-15 minutes to complete.
Data were analysed using multiple regression to examine whether social media use and self-esteem predicted eating concern, shape concern, restraint, bulking, and cutting.

Analyses were conducted in JASP (version 0.95; JASP Team, 2025), and all regression assumptions were met (linearity, normality of residuals, homoscedasticity, independence, and absence of multicollinearity; VIFs = 1.00; Durbin-Watson ≈ 2).

Mean scores were 4.72 (SD = 1.17) for social media use, 1.90 (SD = 0.57) for self-esteem, 5.99 (SD = 6.27) for eating concern, 7.87 (SD = 6.70) for shape concern, 9.83 (SD = 7.19) for restraint, 5.25 (SD = 2.29) for bulking, and 6.63 (SD = 2.51) for cutting.
Bulking was negatively correlated with eating concern, whereas cutting was positively correlated with restraint.
Self-esteem was negatively correlated with eating and shape concern, while social media use was positively correlated only with eating concern.
Eating and shape concern were strongly inter-correlated, and both positively correlated with restraint (see Table 1).

text.text: The correlations informed subsequent exploratory analysis.

The regression model for restraint was not significant, F(2, 73) = 1.28, p = .284, with an 200 adjusted R² of .007, indicating that social media and self-esteem explained less than 1% of the 201 variance.

The models for bulking, F(2, 73) = 1.12, p = .331, adjusted R² = .003, and cutting, F(2, 73) = 0.39, p = .677, adjusted R² = -.016, were not significant, showing that neither predictor accounted for significant variance in these outcomes.
By contrast, the model predicting shape concern was significant, F(2, 73) = 7.17, p = .001, explaining 14.1% of the variance (adjusted R² = .141).
In this model, self-esteem emerged as a significant negative predictor (β = -.38, p < .001), whereas social media use was not significant (β = .14, p = .225).

text.text: The model predicting eating concern was also significant, F(2, 71) = 6.99, p = .002, accounting for 14.1% of the variance (adjusted R² = .141).
Overall, the findings partially support the hypothesis (see Table 2).

text.text: Mediation analysis examined whether self-esteem mediated the relationship between social media use, eating concern, restraint, shape concern, bulking, and cutting.
No significant mediation effects were found for any of the outcome variables (see Fig. 1A, Fig. 1B, Fig. 1C, Fig. 1D, Fig. 1E).

text.text: In all five models, the indirect effect of social media use through self-esteem was not significant (95% confidence intervals for indirect effects all included zero).

The total effects of social media use on each outcome were also not significant (e.g., for eating concern, total effect β = 1.22, 95% CI [-0.20, 2.71] and indirect effect β = -0.07, 95% CI [-0.54, 0.39]).

The results showed that shape concern strongly predicted restraint, and in turn restraint predicted higher cutting tendency.

The indirect effect of shape concern on cutting through restraint was significant (β = 0.078, 95% CI [0.032, 0.138]), while the direct effect of shape concern on cutting was negligible (β = -0.001, 95% CI [-0.092, 0.091]).
This pattern suggests that the correlation between shape concern and cutting was fully accounted for by their mutual relationship with restraint.

In addition to social media use, self-esteem emerged as significant predictor of eating and shape concerns.
This aligns with the transdiagnostic model of eating disorders [26], which conceptualises low self-esteem as a risk factor.

text.text: Lower self-esteem may heighten sensitivity to appearance-based comparisons, increasing shape dissatisfaction and maladaptive eating patterns.
Together, the findings highlight self-esteem as a key psychological mechanism linking body image concerns to eating pathology in young men.
Dietary restraint also emerged as central construct, showing positive associations with both cutting and shape concern, suggesting interconnected processes. [49].

text.text: The exploratory analysis extends this by suggesting that restraint may function as a key pathway linking shape concern to cutting.
This finding echoes previous research emphasising the central role of restraint in the development and maintenance of disordered eating [48].

text.text: Nevertheless, as the mediation model was tested post hoc using cross-sectional data, it should be interpreted cautiously.
Bulking was negatively associated with eating concern, indicating that individuals who bulk may experience fewer eating-related worries.
The absence of direct effects on bulking indicates that this behaviour may be influenced by factors such as athletic identity or gym culture [49].
Consistent with this, a recent meta-analysis [48] concluded that habitual exposure to cultural body norms via social media can increase eating-related preoccupation irrespective of self-esteem.

text.text: Importantly, the current findings should not be interpreted as evidence that social media use universally leads to disordered eating.
Indeed, social media can provide positive outcomes, such as social connection, body satisfaction, and improve emotional well-being [51].
text.formatted: Indeed, social media can provide positive outcomes, such as social connection, body satisfaction, and improve emotional well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">[51]</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, low self-esteem may contribute to body dissatisfaction even in the absence of excessive social media use [52].
text.formatted: Similarly, low self-esteem may contribute to body dissatisfaction even in the absence of excessive social media use <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">[52]</ref>.

text.text: However, the present findings highlight the need for theoretical models of disordered eating to incorporate social media as a distinct influence, as social media use itself may function as an independent risk pathway for eating concern.
The findings have implications for intervention.
Particularly, media literacy interventions may mitigate negative impact of social media.

For example, The Body Project: More than Muscles [53], has demonstrated efficacy in reducing disordered eating and muscle dysmorphia symptoms, and integrating social media literacy into such practice may buffer against eating-related concerns.

text.text: Ultimately, the relationship between social media and disordered eating is likely conditional, as different forms of engagement (e.g., passive scrolling versus active posting, or exposure to fitness content) may exert distinct effects on body image and eating psychopathology [54].

text.text: Several limitations should be acknowledged.
First, the measure of social media use may not have been sufficiently specific to capture exposure to appearance-or fitness-related content.

Prior research indicates that fitness-focused social media content (e.g., "fitspiration") is associated with increased body dissatisfaction and eating pathology [5], and it is therefore possible that a more content-specific measure would have yielded stronger associations.

text.text: Second, the modest sample size limited statistical power for mediation analyses, which typically require larger samples to reliably detect indirect effects [55].

text.text: As such, mediation findings should be interpreted cautiously.

The cross-sectional design limits conclusions about directionality, and longitudinal studies with larger samples are needed to clarify whether social media use contributes to eating psychopathology or reflects maladaptive engagement among already vulnerable individuals.
Additionally, male body concerns may not be fully captured by standard questionnaires, underscoring the need for greater use of male-specific measures in future research [15, 16, 56].

text.text: For that reason, a key strength of the present study is the development and initial validation of the Bulking and Cutting Behaviour Scale.
This measure demonstrated promising psychometric properties and offers a novel tool for assessing bulking and cutting behaviours.
Social media use predicted eating concern, while self-esteem predicted eating and shape concerns.
Neither variable significantly predicted restraint, bulking, or cutting, although bulking was negatively associated with eating concern and cutting positively associated with restraint.
Self-esteem did not mediate associations between social media use and outcomes.
Exploratory analysis showed that restraint fully mediated the relationship between shape concern and cutting, suggesting that cutting may pose higher risk for disordered eating than bulking.
Social media use is linked to body dissatisfaction and disordered eating, but research has mostly focused on women.
Far less is known about its impact on men, particularly in the context of muscularity-oriented behaviours.
Bulking and cutting -increasingly common among young men, and often reinforced by muscular body images online -may represent unexplored pathways to disordered eating [23, 58].

text.text: The study reports the development and initial validation of the Bulking and Cutting Behaviour Scale, a novel measure of muscle-oriented dietary behaviours not captured by existing eating disorder questionnaires.
Combined, the findings support expanding conceptualisations of disordered eating to include bulking and cutting behaviours, which may not align with traditional diagnostic frameworks.
